questions.prompt: A mass m slides on a frictionless floor, tied to a wall by a spring k and a damper b. A force u pushes the mass, and y is its displacement. Which equation describes it?
questions.explanation:
Newton's law: \(m\ddot y=u-b\dot y-ky\). Spring and damper forces oppose displacement and velocity. Rearranged, \(m\ddot y+b\dot y+ky=u\), a linear constant-coefficient ODE, so the system is LTI.
• Adding the spring and damper forces makes them push in the direction of motion, which would be unstable.
• Damping multiplies velocity, and mass multiplies acceleration, not the reverse.
• Dropping \(\ddot y\) ignores inertia.

questions.prompt: A mass-spring-damper has \(m=2\ \mathrm{kg}\), \(b=20\ \mathrm{N\,s/m}\) and \(k=400\ \mathrm{N/m}\). A constant 10 N force is applied. Where does the mass settle, in m?
questions.explanation:
At rest, \(\ddot y=\dot y=0\), so \(ky=u\) and \(y=10/400=0.025\ \mathrm{m}\). Mass and damping set how it gets there, not where it stops.
• \(10/20=0.5\) divides by the damping.
• \(10/2=5\) divides by the mass, which only affects acceleration.

questions.prompt: What is the transfer function from force \(U(s)\) to displacement \(Y(s)\) for \(m\ddot y+b\dot y+ky=u\)?
questions.explanation:
Transforming with zero initial conditions: \((ms^2+bs+k)Y=U\). The inverse polynomial is the transfer function, with units m/N.
• The polynomial without inversion is \(U/Y\).
• An extra s gives force to velocity, not displacement.
• Swapping m and k reverses the coefficients.

questions.prompt: A mass of 0.5 kg hangs on a spring of \(k=200\ \mathrm{N/m}\) with damping \(b=4\ \mathrm{N\,s/m}\). What is its natural frequency \(\omega_n\), in rad/s?
questions.explanation:
\(\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}=\sqrt{400}=20\ \mathrm{rad/s}\), the frequency it would oscillate at with no damping. Gravity only shifts the equilibrium point; it does not change \(\omega_n\).
• \(k/m=400\) forgets the square root.
• \(\sqrt{k}=14.1\) ignores the mass.
• \(\omega_n/(2\pi)=3.18\) is the frequency in Hz.

questions.prompt: For the same system (\(m=0.5\ \mathrm{kg}\), \(k=200\ \mathrm{N/m}\), \(b=4\ \mathrm{N\,s/m}\)), what is the damping ratio \(\zeta=\dfrac{b}{2\sqrt{km}}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(2\sqrt{km}=2\sqrt{100}=20\), so \(\zeta=4/20=0.2\): lightly damped, so expect visible ringing. \(b=20\) would be critical damping.
• \(b/\sqrt{km}=0.4\) forgets the factor 2.
• \(b/(2k)=0.01\) uses the wrong combination.

questions.prompt: A motor shaft has inertia \(J=0.02\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}\) and viscous friction \(c=0.1\ \mathrm{N\,m\,s}\), so its speed obeys \(J\dot\omega+c\omega=\tau\). A constant torque of 0.5 N·m is applied from rest. What speed does it settle to, in rad/s?
questions.explanation:
In steady state \(\dot\omega=0\), so \(\omega=\tau/c=0.5/0.1=5\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). It is a first-order system with time constant \(J/c=0.2\ \mathrm{s}\), the rotational version of a mass with drag.
• \(\tau/J=25\) is the initial acceleration in \(\mathrm{rad/s^2}\), not a speed.
• 0.2 is the time constant.
questions.figure_alt: Shaft speed rising exponentially toward its final value after a torque step.

questions.prompt: A mass-spring-damper with \(m=1\ \mathrm{kg}\), \(b=2\ \mathrm{N\,s/m}\) and \(k=25\ \mathrm{N/m}\) is driven by \(u=3\cos(5t)\) N. What is the steady-state displacement amplitude, in m?
questions.explanation:
\(H(j\omega)=\dfrac{1}{k-m\omega^2+jb\omega}\). At \(\omega=5=\omega_n\), \(k-m\omega^2=0\), so \(|H|=1/(b\omega)=0.1\ \mathrm{m/N}\) and the amplitude is 0.3 m, 2.5 times the static deflection \(3/25=0.12\ \mathrm{m}\). The ratio \(1/(2\zeta)=2.5\) is the resonance gain.
• 0.12 m is the static response.
• \(3/\sqrt{25^2+10^2}\) forgets the \(-m\omega^2\) term.
questions.figure_alt: Bode magnitude from force to displacement: flat, then a resonance peak at 5 rad/s, then falling 40 dB per decade.

questions.prompt: The same system (\(m=1\), \(b=2\), \(k=25\), so \(\zeta=0.2\)) receives a step force. What is the percent overshoot of the displacement?
questions.explanation:
\(M_p=e^{-\pi\zeta/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}=e^{-\pi(0.2)/0.98}=e^{-0.641}=0.527\), so 52.7%. The light damping that gave the large resonance peak also gives large overshoot: both describe the same pair of poles.
• \(e^{-\pi\zeta}=53.3\%\) drops the square root.
• 20% treats \(\zeta\) as the overshoot.
questions.figure_alt: Step response of the displacement: large overshoot and decaying ringing.

questions.prompt: In a mass-spring-damper, the mass is doubled while k and b stay the same. How do \(\omega_n\) and \(\zeta\) change?
options: Both fall by a factor of \(\sqrt2\)
questions.explanation:
\(\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}\) and \(\zeta=b/(2\sqrt{km})\): both have \(\sqrt m\) in the denominator. A heavier mass rings more slowly and with relatively less damping.
• \(\zeta\) depends on m too.
• Square roots, not linear factors.
• More mass never raises \(\omega_n\).

questions.prompt: Preview of second-order systems. For \(m=1\), \(b=2\), \(k=25\) (poles at \(-1\pm j\sqrt{24}\)), at what time does the step response reach its first peak, in s?
questions.explanation:
The first peak comes half a damped period after the step: \(t_p=\pi/\omega_d=\pi/4.90=0.641\ \mathrm{s}\).
• \(\pi/\omega_n=0.628\ \mathrm{s}\) uses the undamped frequency.
• \(2\pi/\omega_d=1.28\ \mathrm{s}\) is a full period.

questions.prompt: Preview of system identification. A lightly damped 2 kg mass on an unknown spring is tapped, and it rings with a period of 0.5 s. Estimate the spring constant \(k\approx m(2\pi/T)^2\), in N/m.
questions.explanation:
Light damping means \(\omega_d\approx\omega_n=2\pi/T=12.57\ \mathrm{rad/s}\), so \(k=m\omega_n^2=2\times158=316\ \mathrm{N/m}\). Reading parameters off a measured response is the basic idea of identification.
• \(m(2\pi/T)=25\) forgets to square.
• \(m/T^2=8\) forgets the \(2\pi\).

questions.prompt: Preview of cruise control. A 1200 kg car with linearized drag \(b=60\ \mathrm{N\,s/m}\) obeys \(m\dot v+bv=F\). Starting from steady speed, an extra 600 N of drive force is applied. How much has the speed increased after 20 s, in m/s?
questions.explanation:
First order: time constant \(m/b=20\ \mathrm{s}\) and final change \(F/b=10\ \mathrm{m/s}\). After one time constant, \(10(1-e^{-1})=6.32\ \mathrm{m/s}\).
• 10 m/s is the final change, reached only after several time constants.
• \(F/m\cdot20=10\) assumes the acceleration stays constant, ignoring the growing drag.
